title: RBI raises the cost of rupee hedges after corporate forward buying hits record
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India barred rebooking of cancelled rupee derivatives and imposed a 20% cash reserve on certain FX contracts — after corporate forward-dollar purchases surged to a record $77 billion in September.
body:
• What the RBI did: On Saturday, the Reserve Bank of India barred firms from rebooking cancelled rupee-linked foreign exchange derivatives, slashed the threshold for transactions done without establishing underlying exposure, and required banks to set aside 20% cash against certain FX contracts.
  • The scale of the rush: Corporate purchases of forward dollars hit a record $77 billion in September, up 80% from a year earlier, while corresponding sales were subdued at $41 billion — a one-sided hedging wave that itself became a drag on the currency, six bankers told Reuters.
  • The cost impact: The measures could raise hedging costs by 80 to 150 basis points, depending on how much banks pass on to clients — the fixed paisa margins banks used to charge are no longer feasible.
  • What this means for you: A rupee near record lows — 96.96 last week, down nearly 7% this year, Asia's worst-performing currency — stretches every dollar an NRI sends home into more rupees, but it also raises costs for importers and for anyone hedging future payments. If you have dollar-denominated obligations to meet in rupees, expect hedging to cost you more now; if you're remitting to India, the rate tailwind is historically strong.

The RBI moves from signaling to squeezing

The Indian central bank's latest measures to support the plunging rupee will raise the cost of buying protection against further weakness and slow a hedging surge that had become an additional drag on the currency, six bankers told Reuters. The rupee fell near its all-time low of 96.96 against the dollar last week, despite $140 billion raised via special dollar deposit schemes and higher interest rates — evidence of how hard the Reserve Bank of India is finding it to stabilize the currency.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=lWJGSIZEFPo

The market response was immediate. The rupee opened at 95.76 on Monday, up about 1% from Friday's close of 96.73, making it a standout performer in Asia's foreign-exchange markets.

The mechanism: why hedging pressure feeds on itself

Here is how the curbs work. When importers expect the rupee to weaken further, they rush to buy forward dollars — locking in today's rate to protect against higher future costs. That hedging demand is itself dollar demand: it pushes the rupee down further. Expectations of depreciation lead to more hedging, which leads to more weakness — a self-reinforcing cycle that bankers say was amplifying the rupee's slide.

The RBI's package attacks that cycle at three points. Barring the rebooking of cancelled rupee-linked derivative contracts makes it harder for companies to repeatedly cancel and roll positions. Slashing the threshold for transactions without underlying exposure raises the documentation bar. And the 20% cash reserve requirement forces banks to park capital against large hedges, raising their cost of offering forward contracts — a cost that flows through to clients as an 80–150 basis-point increase.

Context & Background

The rupee's slide has two engines: surging oil prices and heavy foreign outflows from Indian equities, which have pulled the currency down nearly 7% this year — the worst performance in the region. India imports most of its crude, so elevated crude prices feed directly into the import bill.

Alongside the hedging curbs, the RBI opened a special window through which oil marketing companies — one of the largest sources of daily dollar demand — can buy dollars directly from the central bank, diverting their purchases from the regular market. The central bank's reserves had already fallen $12.95 billion to $734.60 billion in the week ended October 2, the fourth straight weekly decline.

"The RBI's measures represent a virtual shutdown of the market. The dollar demand from hedging and from the oil companies will now exit the market."

— Anil Kumar Bhansali, Finrex Treasury Advisors

Mitul Kotecha, head of FX and EM macro strategy for Asia at Barclays, said in a note that the RBI has moved from merely signaling the rupee's weakness may be excessive to directly restraining dollar demand and speculative activity — though he added that the measures change where and when dollars are purchased, rather than the underlying demand from oil imports, trade flows and capital outflows, and that his outlook remains for an orderly depreciation.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The rally has not changed the underlying arithmetic. Despite the 1% jump, the rupee is still down 6.6% this year. The curbs caught the market off guard — bankers worked through the weekend to have systems in place for Monday's open — and forward premiums are expected to swing as corporates rework their hedging strategies.

Lasting stability, analysts note, will depend on crude oil prices, foreign portfolio flows, and the direction of the global dollar — none of which the RBI controls. Read the full Reuters report on the hedging curbs and its follow-up on the rupee's rally for the complete picture.
